operations.name: Adolph Ersson

expected.name: Adolph Ersson
expected.description:
Adolph Ersson was one of the 74 Industrial Workers of the World members held in the Snohomish County jail and charged with murder after the Everett Massacre. On November 5, 1916, some 300 Industrial Workers of the World members sailed from Seattle to Everett, Washington aboard the steamers Verona and Calista to support a shingle-weavers' strike and the IWW's free-speech fight. At the Everett dock, Snohomish County sheriff Donald McRae and a posse of armed vigilantes opened fire on the Verona, killing at least five Wobblies and wounding dozens. The returning IWW members were arrested, and 74 were charged with the murder of two deputies (Jefferson Beard and Charles Curtis) killed in the gunfire. Only Thomas H. Tracy was brought to trial; after his acquittal on May 5, 1917, the charges against the others were dropped. At the time of the massacre he was 26, a laborer and sailor, born in Sweden.

From Kenyon Zimmer's Red Scare Deportees index (kenyonzimmer.com, compiled from INS deportation case files): Active in union and strike activity in Australia after emigrating there. Then migrated to the U, where he joined the IWW in Denver in 1914. Survivor of the 1916 Everett Massacre; arrested in its aftermath and held until charges were dropped in 1917. Arrested again in Seattle in October 1918 and in Los Angeles in May 1919. Deported on June 26, 1919.

After deportation made his way to Norway, where gave speeches about the repression of the IWW in the US. Found work on a ship sailing from Kristiana to New York, where he jumped ship in December 1919. 1924 working as a laborer in Buffalo. At some point he returned to Sweden, where he died in 1967.

operations.name: Amy Schechter

expected.name: Amy Schechter
expected.description: Amy Schechter was a Workers International Relief organizer and one of the three women charged with murder. Amy Schechter was one of the sixteen Gastonia defendants held in the Gaston County jail on the first-degree murder charge — facing the electric chair — after the 7 June 1929 killing of Police Chief Aderholt. The murder charge against the defendants outside the convicted seven was dropped before the October retrial. On 7 June 1929, police attacked the National Textile Workers Union tent colony at the Loray Mill in Gastonia, North Carolina, and Police Chief O. F. Aderholt was killed in the exchange of fire. Sixteen strikers and organizers were charged with his murder — a frame-up, the defense held, aimed at breaking the communist-led Southern textile drive. The International Labor Defense mounted a national campaign for the Gastonia defendants.
expected.body:
1920s custody-date review: The Daily Worker of August 3, 1929, page 1, carries Liston Oak's Gastonia dispatch dated August 2. It names Amy Schechter, Vera Buch and Sophie Melvin, states that all three had been jailed since the June 7 shooting, and reports their completed release that day on ,000 bail each. This establishes August 2 as their bail-release date, not the later dismissal of charges. Vera Buch is also spelled Bush in the headline. The separate later proceedings in Sophie Melvin's record are unchanged.

Sources: Daily Worker, August 3, 1929, page 1; June 8 Gastonia Gazette report, transcribed by ANCHOR, independently naming Schechter and Bush among those arrested the preceding night. Existing portraits retained.

operations.research_note: Grandnephew Dave Schechter reports August 4, 1892 birthday based on family and FBI/Soviet archival research. Death year 1962 corroborated independently but no exact day proposed.

expected.name: Erasmo Abate
expected.description:
Erasmo Abate was born 1895 in Formia, Italy. Worked as a construction worker, house painter, editor. Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Secretary of Philadelphia’s anarcho-syndicalist Union of Italian Workers, which collaborated with the IWW, he became the editor of the anarchist paper La Comune (1911–1915) and edited La Conquista (1920–1921). Arrested on May 25, 1921; deported on January 7, 1922. His wife and child remained in the United States.

In Italy, Abate was sent by Errico Malatesta to aid the antifascist movement in Ancona, where he helped lead the local section of the Arditi del Popolo. Later he fled arrest to Paris, where he was active in the exiled Comitato di Azione and involved in the “Garibaldi Affair,” a planned armed anti-Mussolini expedition led by Ricciotti Garibaldi, from which Abate withdrew shortly before Garibaldi was exposed as a fascist agent.

In 1926 Abate reentered the United States illegally under the name Hugo Roland, rejoined his family, briefly edited the anarchist newspaper Germinal (1926) in Chicago, and later settled in Michigan. Although a controversial and marginalized figure due his involvement in the Garibaldi Affair, Abate remained active in the anarchist movement in the US until his death in 1977.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
